stages.sub: How the Lorenz curve is turned into a single number, and what that number can and cannot tell you.

steps.q: On the Lorenz diagram, a country's curve bows far away from the 45-degree line. Picture the sliver of space trapped between the curve and that line, compared with the whole triangle under the line. If inequality were even worse, would that trapped sliver take up a bigger or smaller share of the triangle?
steps.hint: More bowing means the curve strays further from the line, so the gap between them grows.

But one collects income data mainly from formal tax records, missing large informal-sector earnings, and neither figure tells you whether the inequality comes from education gaps, discrimination, or something else. Does the single number capture all of this detail?

steps.q: One country sits on vast oil and mineral deposits while its neighbour has almost no valuable land or minerals at all. If both countries otherwise work equally hard, would you expect their measured inequality between each other to be the same?
steps.right: No, the oil-rich country likely ends up richer
steps.wrong: Yes, hard work alone decides the outcome
steps.hint: Think about what one country can sell to the world that the other simply does not have.
